extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of aesthetics, art theory, and visual arts (painters, sculptors, critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for producing and judging sculpture, painting, and related visual arts, with comparisons to poetry and stage acting. Emphasises what is appropriate to each medium, the priority of the Idea over the concept, and the rejection of allegory/symbolism in plastic and pictorial art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression limited by medium (shriek example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of shrieking, and consequently its effect upon the onlooker, lies entirely in sound; not in the distortion of the mouth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt in sculpture to represent violent vocal expressions (e.g., a shrieking mouth) because the medium cannot reproduce sound; representing the physical means (distorted mouth) without the sound would disturb other features, sacrifice overall expression and beauty, and produce the spectacle of a continuous effort without effect (ridiculous). In contrast, poetry and acting (which include sound and imagination) may represent shrieking effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture prefers nakedness; drapery only to exhibit form
rubrics_metrics.description: Because beauty accompanied with grace is the principal object of sculpture, it loves nakedness, and allows clothing only so far as it does not conceal the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use drapery in sculpture not as covering but as a means of exhibiting the underlying form—drapery should be a suggestion that forces the understanding to perceive the body's form. Excessive clothing that conceals the form is contrary to the aims of sculpture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drapery and foreshortening as perceptual suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drapery in sculpture is in a certain sense what foreshortening is in painting: both are suggestions that, when successful, force the understanding to perceive what is suggested as if it were actually given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat drapery and foreshortening as devices to enable the spectator to infer the body/form; they must be used so they lead the mind to perceive the underlying idea rather than merely decorate or obscure it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitory movement may be represented in motionless art
rubrics_metrics.description: A merely passing state incapable of duration ought not to be excluded from motionless works of art; many excellent figures are fixed in merely transitory movements (dancing, wrestling, catching, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject fleeting actions as unsuitable for painting or sculpture; artists may and should capture transient movements when they serve to express the Idea. Examples include dance and athletic poses successfully frozen in art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical painting's principal object: character
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical painting has for its principal object, besides beauty and grace, character — the representation of will at the highest grade of its objectification, when the individual exhibits a particular side of the Idea of humanity in bearing, occupation, and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose scenes and representative individuals that reveal the many-sidedness of the Idea of man; focus on characters whose bearing and actions make the universal human Idea visible, not merely on outward historical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer inward significance (perceptible Idea) over outward/nominative significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The inward significance is the depth of insight into the Idea of man which an action reveals (art's concern); the outward significance is historical importance (belongs to history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects for painting based on their inward (real, perceptible) significance that can be apprehended by the spectator, rather than their outward (nominal) historical importance which may only be reached by thought. A picture should present what is perceptible, not rely on learned costume or backstory to supply meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose historical subjects only if their chief point is representable
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those historical subjects are to be chosen the chief point of which can actually be represented, and not merely arrived at by thought; otherwise the nominal significance is too remote from the real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid historical topics where the important element is only inferable or conceptual; ensure the pivotal significance of the subject can be made perceptible in the composition, or else the picture's real artistic value will be compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confining art to poor or arbitrarily assigned subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical subjects become distinctly disadvantageous when they confine the painter to a field chosen for reasons other than artistic suitability, especially when that field is poor in picturesque and significant objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let patronage, tradition, or narrow subject constraints force the artist into depicting scenes that lack picturesque or inward significance (e.g., narrow, obscure historical groups); choose subjects that provide material for revealing the Idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/biblical subjects: value depends on picturable ethical spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Testament (and much subsequent church history) is often unsuitable for painting; yet where the ethical spirit of Christianity is made perceptible—groups of saints showing the surrender of will and perfect knowledge—these are the highest achievements of painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious subjects should be judged by whether they perceptibly express the inner spirit (resignation, knowledge) of Christianity; if they merely recreate historical or nominal elements they are less artistically valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's object is the Idea, not the concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of art is an Idea (in Plato’s sense) — an object of perception, though representing many particulars; the concept is abstract, discursive, and barren in art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic works should aim to communicate a perceptible, determined Idea that can be apprehended by the spectator; avoid starting from or making the communication of an abstract concept the aim of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject works that start from the concept (imitators/mannerists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitators and mannerists start, in art, from the concept: they fix what pleases in a concept and imitate it dexterously, but cannot impart inner life to a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value originality arising from direct apprehension of life and nature; treat mannerism and imitation as parasitic and ephemeral. The artist should work from immediate feeling/Idea, not from consciously copied conceptual formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring art springs from direct apprehension of life (originality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine and immortal works of art spring only from direct apprehension of life and nature by genius; such works belong to humanity and cannot grow old, unlike mannered works tied to the spirit of an age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for works that are drawn from life and the world so they possess 'eternal youth' — these will be recognised slowly by a few capable judges and survive posterity's test; avoid art that appeals only to contemporary concepts and fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory and symbolism are foreign to plastic and pictorial art
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegory (a work meaning something different from what it represents) draws the beholder away from the expressed perceptible Idea to an abstract conception; in plastic and pictorial art this is a mistake and often injures perceptible truth. Symbolism (conventional signs like rose=secrecy) is like hieroglyphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject allegory and conventional symbolic emblems in sculpture and painting when they serve conceptual ends rather than presenting a perceptible Idea. If a pictorial work happens to be allegorical yet possesses artistic value, that value lies outside its function as allegory. Avoid bizarre or forced symbols (e.g., tortoise for feminine seclusion) that have no natural connection to what is represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific allowance: allegory and tropes in poetry/language arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry and the arts of language the conception is the immediately given material; therefore similes, metaphors, parables, and allegories are permissible and often highly effective to call up perceptible images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply different standards across media: while allegory is generally to be rejected in pictorial/plastic arts, it is serviceable and appropriate in poetry and literary arts, where the medium starts from abstract conception and can lead the imagination to perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent characteristic occupations without violent distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Painted or sculptured representations of characteristic occupations (e.g., St. Cecilia at the organ, Raphael's violin-player) are permissible provided they demand no violent movement of the body or distortion of the mouth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict habits/occupations as identifying traits when they do not require physical distortions that conflict with beauty or the medium's limits. Favor compositional elements that suggest character through posture or objects rather than grotesque or impossible physical distortion.
